Hey Indaelcio - you are registered for tax and payroll using your passport number - the tofes 101 tax form that all employees in Israel fill out every year allows for this. 

You aren't eligible for resident tax credit points until you get an A5 visa - although on a B1, most people see still much less come out of their salary compared to residents, as most B1 visa holders not be making full bituach leumi and health insurance payments (there can be exceptions depending on your country of origin - certain countries (mostly European countries) have bilateral agreements with Israel, and therefore citizens of those countries are eligible for additional coverage and will have to pay.) 

Your tax residency mainly depends on how long you have been in Israel - if you have been here 183 days in a tax year you will be considered a resident. But note that this does not affect whether you have to pay tax from your work in Israel (as even non-tax residents have to pay income tax on income from Israeli sources). 

You should make sure your workplace sets up a pension account for you (B1 visa holders are legally entitled to this), and you should also ask if they can pay for your private health insurance - it is a bit legally unclear whether they have to, so there is a chance they will say no - but you can try. You can read a bit more about employment and social rights on our website here: https://aic.org.il/understanding-the-israeli-pay-slip-taxation-and-social-rights/
